q: Two threads run inside the same process. Which of these does each thread get its own separate copy of?
options: Objects allocated on the heap
Global variables
Its call stack: local variables and return addresses
Its table of open files, so a file one thread opens stays private
why: Threads of one process share the address space: code, globals, the heap and open files. What each thread owns is its execution state: registers, program counter and its own stack, so local variables in one thread's calls are separate.
wrong: The heap belongs to the process, so any thread holding a pointer can reach the same object.
Globals live once in the process's memory and every thread sees the same variable.
File descriptors are per process; a file one thread opens can be read by another.

q: A C server handles each request on its own thread. One thread dereferences a NULL pointer. What happens to the other requests in flight?
options: They are lost: the segfault ends the whole process
They finish normally: only the faulty thread is stopped
They pause until the OS restarts the faulty thread from its start
Each other thread gets an error code back from its next system call
why: A segmentation fault is delivered to the process, and the default action ends the process. Threads share one address space, so the OS cannot tell whether memory is still sane and does not keep the other threads alive.
wrong: That is how an uncaught exception in one Java thread looks. A memory fault in C ends the whole process.
The OS does not restart threads; restarting is the program's or a supervisor's job.
There is no per-thread error code; the other threads simply stop with the process.

q: How many times does this C program print hi? Assume every fork() succeeds.
why: fork() clones the calling process, and the child continues from the same point, loop counter included. Each round doubles the number of processes: 1, 2, 4, 8. All 8 reach the printf.
wrong: That counts fork calls in the original process only; children keep running the loop too.
That assumes children skip the rest of the loop. A child continues right after fork, so it forks as well.
That counts the children only. The original process also reaches the printf.

q: The child sets x to 10 and exits; the parent waits for it and then prints x. What does this print?
options: 5 or 10, depending on which process the scheduler runs first
Two lines: 10, then 5
why: After fork() the child has its own copy of the parent's memory. Changing x in the child changes only the child's copy, so the parent still sees 5.
wrong: That would be true for threads, which share memory. A forked child writes to its own copy.
Timing cannot matter here: the processes do not share x at all, and wait() orders them anyway.
The child calls exit(0) inside the if, so it never reaches the printf.

q: A thread sets the global counter to 10. The main thread waits for it with pthread_join, then prints counter. What does this print?
options: 0 or 10, depending on which thread the scheduler runs first
Nothing: it does not compile, a thread cannot write a global that main reads
why: Threads share the process's globals, so the write is visible to main. pthread_join waits until the thread has finished, so the write has already happened when main prints.
wrong: That is process behaviour after fork. Threads see the same global, not a copy.
pthread_join blocks main until the thread is done, so the order is fixed.
Any thread may read or write a global; C has no such rule.

q: Why is creating a new thread usually cheaper than creating a new process?
options: A thread is created without involving the kernel at all
A new process must copy every byte of the parent's memory before it can run
It joins an existing address space and needs only a stack and registers
Threads are always placed on a core that is already idle
why: A process needs its own address space, page tables and resource tables. A thread joins an address space that already exists, so the OS only sets up a stack and an execution context.
wrong: OS threads are created through a system call; the saving is in what the kernel has to build.
Modern fork shares pages copy-on-write, so it does not copy everything up front. It is still more work than a thread.
Creation cost has nothing to do with core placement; the scheduler decides that later.

q: Your app runs plugins written by third parties, in C. A buggy plugin must not be able to crash or corrupt the app. What should each plugin run in?
options: A separate process, talking to the app through IPC
A thread, so it can share the app's data without copying
A thread, because a crash in a thread stays inside that thread
The main thread, wrapped in a try/catch around each plugin call
why: A separate process has its own address space, so a bad pointer in the plugin can only damage the plugin's memory, and if it crashes the app keeps running. The price is slower communication through IPC.
wrong: Sharing memory is exactly the danger: a buggy plugin could overwrite the app's data.
A segfault in any thread ends the whole process, the app included.
try/catch handles exceptions, not memory faults or silent corruption from a bad pointer.

q: A C++ app on an 8-core machine must resize 8 large images and put the results into one in-memory gallery. Which approach fits best?
options: 8 processes, because threads of one process cannot run on different cores at once
8 threads: they run in parallel and write into the shared gallery without copying
One thread, because switching between threads would cost more than it saves
8 processes, because child processes share the parent's heap automatically
why: The work is CPU-heavy and splits into independent parts, and the results end up in one shared structure. Threads run on separate cores in parallel and see the same memory, so nothing has to be copied between processes.
wrong: The OS schedules the threads of one process on all cores at once; a process is not tied to a single core.
With 8 cores and 8 threads, each thread can have a core; there is little switching and an 8x speedup is possible.
Processes do not share heap memory; results would have to be sent back through IPC.

q: A C function declares a local array int a[100] and also calls malloc for 100 ints. It returns without calling free. What happens to the two blocks of memory?
options: Both are released automatically when the function returns
The array goes on return; the malloc block stays until free or exit
The malloc block is released on return; the local array stays until the program ends
Neither is released until the process exits
why: Locals live in the function's stack frame, which is popped on return. Heap memory from malloc has no owner frame: it stays allocated until free is called, and if the pointer is lost it leaks until the process ends.
wrong: Only stack memory follows function scope. The heap block outlives the pointer variable that held it.
That is reversed: the stack frame is popped, while the heap block remains.
The stack frame is reused as soon as the function returns, so the local array is gone at once.

q: What is the main purpose of virtual memory?
options: To give each process its own private address space
To make memory access faster than reading RAM directly
It is a file on disk that is used instead of RAM once RAM is full
To let several processes write into each other's variables more easily
why: With virtual memory every process sees its own address space. The OS and hardware translate those addresses to physical memory, which isolates processes from each other and lets the OS place, share or move pages to disk freely.
wrong: Translation adds work to each access; speed comes from caches, not from virtual memory.
That describes swap space, one thing virtual memory makes possible, not virtual memory itself.
The opposite: separate address spaces stop processes from touching each other's memory.

q: After fork, the child sets x to 2 and the parent keeps 1. Each prints x and its address; the child prints first. What do the two lines show?
options: Two different addresses, because two processes cannot use the same address
The same address and the value 2 on both lines
The same address, with 2 in the child's line and 1 in the parent's
Only one line, because the parent is still blocked in wait() when the child exits
why: Addresses a program sees are virtual. After fork both processes use the same virtual address for x, but each address space maps it to its own physical memory, so the values differ.
wrong: Each process has its own address space, so the same virtual address can exist in both.
Equal addresses do not mean shared memory here; each process translates the address to its own page.
wait() returns once the child exits, and then the parent prints its own line.

q: Why does the OS give memory to processes in fixed-size pages rather than as one contiguous block per process?
options: Pages can sit in any free frames, so no process needs one large free gap
Reading memory in whole pages is faster than reading it one byte at a time
Pages let the compiler choose where in physical RAM each variable will live
Without pages a program could never use more than one megabyte of memory
why: With pages, a process's memory can be scattered across any free frames, and the page table hides that. Contiguous blocks leave holes between processes that may be too small for the next request.
wrong: Paging is about how memory is mapped, not a faster way to read it; each access still goes byte or word at a time.
The compiler only sees virtual addresses. The OS decides the physical frames at run time.
Contiguous allocation can hand out large blocks too; it just fragments over time.

q: Under memory pressure, the OS moved part of a program's array to disk. Later the program reads that part of the array. What happens?
options: The program crashes with a segmentation fault
The read returns an error code, and the program has to reload the data itself
The CPU reads the value straight from the disk without bringing it into RAM
A page fault: the kernel loads the page into RAM, then the read runs again
why: The page table marks the page as not present, so the access traps into the kernel. The kernel reads the page from disk into a free frame, fixes the mapping and resumes the program at the same instruction. The program only sees a delay.
wrong: A segfault is for addresses the program has no right to use. This page is valid, just not in RAM.
Paging is invisible to the program; a plain memory read has no error code to return.
The CPU can only work on data in RAM; the page must be loaded first.

q: A teammate sees thousands of page faults per second in a healthy service and says it must be full of memory bugs. What is the best reply?
options: Right: every page fault is an access to an invalid address
Page faults only happen when RAM is full, so the machine needs more memory
They are normal; only a forbidden address turns into a segfault
Page faults mean a RAM chip is failing and should be replaced
why: The OS loads pages lazily: on first touch of new heap, stack or code, and for pages that were swapped out. Each of those is a page fault the kernel handles silently. Only an access to an unmapped or forbidden address turns into a crash.
wrong: Most page faults are valid accesses to pages that just are not mapped in yet.
First-touch faults happen even with plenty of free RAM, because pages are set up on demand.
A page fault is a normal software event, not a hardware error report.

q: A recursive C function, built without optimizations, has a bug: for some input it never reaches its base case. What eventually happens?
options: It runs forever, because function calls do not use memory
The heap fills up, because each call frame is allocated with malloc
The OS keeps growing the stack into all free RAM, so the program slows down but never stops
Each call adds a stack frame; the stack hits its size limit and the program crashes
why: Every call pushes a frame holding locals and the return address. A thread's stack has a maximum size, so unbounded recursion runs past it, touches a guard area and the program is killed with a stack overflow. (An optimizing compiler may turn some recursion into a loop, which is why the build matters.)
wrong: Each call needs a frame for its locals and return address, so memory use grows with depth.
Call frames live on the stack, not the heap; malloc is not involved.
The stack size is capped (by default often 8 MB for the main thread on Linux), so the crash comes long before RAM runs out.

q: In C, a function with a local array int buf[10000000] (about 40 MB) crashes as soon as it is called, but malloc of 40 MB works. Why?
options: Local arrays are zeroed first, and that takes so long the OS kills the program
The stack has a small default size limit, while the heap can grow far larger
The stack lives in the CPU cache, which only holds a few megabytes
An array larger than one page cannot be placed on the stack
why: A thread's stack is limited to a few megabytes by default (commonly 8 MB on Linux, 1 MB on Windows; configurable, but small). A 40 MB local overruns it at once. The heap is limited only by available memory, so large buffers belong there.
wrong: C does not zero local arrays, and slowness would not cause a crash.
The stack is ordinary memory in RAM; caches hold copies of any memory, stack or heap.
Stack frames can span many pages; the problem is the total stack limit, not page size.

q: What does the OS actually do during a context switch from thread A to thread B?
options: Saves A's registers and program counter, then loads B's saved ones
Writes all of A's memory to disk so B can use the RAM
Restarts B from the beginning of its code
Moves A to a different CPU core so that B can run on this core instead
why: The CPU only holds one execution state at a time. The kernel stores A's registers, program counter and stack pointer, then restores B's, so B continues exactly where it stopped.
wrong: That is swapping, which is a separate and much rarer event; A's memory stays in RAM.
B resumes from its saved program counter, not from the start.
Moving a thread to another core is a scheduling choice, not what a switch does.

q: Saving and loading registers takes only a few hundred instructions, yet context switches are considered expensive. What is the main hidden cost?
options: The kernel must reload the next program from its executable file
All open files of the old task are flushed to disk
Caches hold the old task's data, so the new one starts slowly
The CPU must reset itself before running a different task
why: After a switch, the data the new task needs is often not in the caches, which are full of the previous task's data. It runs with many cache misses for a while. A switch between processes also changes the memory mapping, which adds more of these misses.
wrong: The program is already in memory; only its saved state is restored.
A context switch does not touch files; open files stay as they are.
No reset happens; the kernel just swaps the execution state.

q: Which context switch is usually cheaper, and why?
options: Two processes: a thread switch must synchronize the threads first
Two threads of one process: the memory mapping stays the same
Same cost either way: only registers are saved in both cases
Two processes: a thread switch must also copy the shared heap
why: Threads of one process share an address space, so a switch between them leaves the memory mapping and much of the cached data valid. A process switch must also install a new address space, and the new process finds little of its data in the caches.
wrong: A switch does not need synchronization between the threads; the kernel just saves one state and loads another.
A process switch also changes the address space, which costs more than saving registers.
Shared memory is not copied on any switch; threads already see the same heap.

q: A CPU-bound job on a 4-core machine is split into 2000 threads instead of 4. It finishes noticeably slower. What is the most likely reason?
options: Only 4 run at once; the rest just add switches and cache misses
The OS runs threads strictly in creation order, so the later ones wait
Each thread receives a smaller share of RAM, so the work spills to disk
This cannot happen: more threads always means more work done in parallel
why: With 4 cores, at most 4 CPU-bound threads make progress at once. The other 1996 add context switches and push each other's data out of the caches, so more time goes to overhead and less to the work.
wrong: Schedulers share the CPU among ready threads by time slices, not by creation order.
RAM is not split per thread. Each extra thread costs only a stack, not a share of memory.
Parallelism is capped by the cores. Past that, extra CPU-bound threads only add overhead.

q: Why can't a normal application send commands directly to the disk controller?
options: It runs in user mode, where the CPU blocks direct device access
Disks are too slow to be controlled directly by application code
Only programs written in assembly can reach the hardware
The compiler strips out any instruction that touches hardware
why: The CPU has privilege levels. Apps run in user mode, so the hardware refuses device and privileged operations from them. They must ask the kernel through a system call, which checks permissions and protects other programs' data.
wrong: Speed is not the reason; the restriction is about protection.
Assembly code in user mode faces the same CPU checks; the language does not matter.
The compiler can emit such instructions; the CPU traps them at run time in user mode.

q: Which of these operations needs a system call?
options: Sorting an array that is already in memory
Computing the length of a string with strlen
Adding two integers in a tight loop
Fetching 4 KB of a file from the disk
why: A file lives on a device that only the kernel may touch, so reading it requires asking the kernel. The other three work only on the process's own memory and run entirely in user mode.
wrong: Sorting reads and writes the process's own memory, which needs no kernel help.
strlen is a library function that runs in user space; being in the C library does not make it a system call.
Arithmetic is ordinary CPU work in user mode.

q: A program calls read() on a file. Which sequence best describes what happens?
options: The program jumps straight into the kernel's read code, like any normal function call
A trap enters kernel mode; the kernel checks, reads, and returns to user mode
The kernel copies the program into kernel memory and runs it there until read() finishes
The program switches into kernel mode and stays there for the rest of its run
why: The library places the arguments in registers and executes a trap instruction. The CPU switches to kernel mode and enters the kernel at a fixed, trusted entry point. The kernel validates the arguments, does the work, and returns to user mode at the next instruction.
wrong: A normal call cannot raise privilege; the trap is what enters the kernel at a safe, fixed point.
Only the request crosses over; the program itself stays in its own memory.
The CPU returns to user mode as soon as the system call is done.

q: Program A writes a 1 MB file with one write() system call per byte. Program B uses buffered fwrite, which issues a few large write() calls. Why is A much slower?
options: The disk has to spin and write once for every single write() call
write() is limited to one byte per call, so it needs special handling
fwrite is compiled to faster machine code than write()
Each write() is a trip into the kernel, paid a million times
why: A system call is far more expensive than a normal function call: a mode switch plus the kernel's checks and bookkeeping. Buffering collects many bytes in user memory and pays that cost a few times instead of a million.
wrong: The kernel caches writes in memory and sends them to the disk later; it is not one disk operation per call.
write() accepts any number of bytes; A simply chooses to send one at a time.
fwrite still ends in write() calls. It is faster because it makes far fewer of them.

q: A buggy program passes an invalid buffer pointer to read(). What does a correct kernel do?
options: Write the data anyway, since kernel mode may access any address
Ignore the pointer and silently drop the data
Crash the whole machine, because the kernel touched a bad address
Check the address and fail the call with an error
why: The kernel never trusts values coming from user mode. It checks that the buffer is memory the process is allowed to write, and if not the call fails with an error (EFAULT on Linux). The program is not given a way to make the kernel write over memory it does not own.
wrong: Writing blindly would let a program use the kernel to overwrite memory it does not own.
The program is told the call failed; silently dropping data would hide the bug.
Validating user pointers exists so a bad argument cannot take the system down.

q: A program on a modern desktop OS enters an infinite loop that does no I/O. Other apps stay responsive. What makes this possible?
options: The looping program gives up the CPU on its own at each loop iteration
A timer interrupt hands the CPU back to the kernel
The OS detects infinite loops and terminates them
Every program gets its own dedicated CPU core
why: The scheduler is preemptive. A hardware timer interrupts the CPU at regular intervals and enters the kernel, which can then switch to another thread whether or not the looping program cooperates.
wrong: A plain loop never yields. Relying on that is cooperative scheduling, where this loop would freeze others.
The OS cannot tell an infinite loop from a long computation, so it does not try.
There are usually far more runnable programs than cores; they share them through time slices.

q: In a cooperative system, each task runs until it gives the CPU back by itself. What is the main risk?
options: One task that never yields can freeze every other task
A task can be interrupted between any two instructions
Tasks switch far more often than in a preemptive system
Each task needs its own copy of the kernel
why: Nothing forces a switch in a cooperative system. If one task loops or blocks without yielding, no other task gets the CPU. Preemptive schedulers fix this with timer interrupts.
wrong: That describes preemption. In a cooperative system a task is only switched where it chooses to yield.
It usually switches less, since switches only happen when a task yields.
The scheduling style does not change how many kernels there are.

q: A round robin scheduler can use a very short time slice (microseconds) or a very long one (seconds). What goes wrong at each extreme?
options: Short: tasks starve. Long: the CPU sits idle between slices
Short: interactive apps lag behind. Long: too much time goes to context switches
Short: CPU time goes to switching. Long: it acts like first come first served
Nothing: slice size changes fairness but not overall performance
why: Every slice ends in a context switch, so tiny slices spend much of the CPU on switching. Huge slices mean a task may wait seconds for its turn, which is first come first served in practice and makes interactive apps feel frozen.
wrong: Round robin gives every task a turn, so none starves, and a long slice does not leave the CPU idle.
That is reversed: short slices are the costly ones, long slices are the laggy ones.
Switch overhead and waiting time both depend directly on slice size.

q: A strict priority scheduler always runs the highest-priority ready job. High-priority jobs keep arriving, so a low-priority job never runs. What is this, and what is a common fix?
options: Deadlock; kill one of the high-priority jobs
Starvation; give the low-priority job a longer time slice when it runs
Thrashing; add more RAM
Starvation; raise a job's priority the longer it waits
why: A job that is ready but never chosen is starving. Aging fixes it: the longer a job waits, the higher its priority grows, until it is eventually picked.
wrong: Deadlock is tasks waiting for each other. Here the job is ready and simply never picked.
A longer slice does not help a job that never gets picked in the first place.
Thrashing is about memory and paging, not about which job gets the CPU.

q: A text editor (mostly waiting for keystrokes) and a video encoder (always computing) share one core. Why does the scheduler run the editor first whenever it becomes ready?
options: The editor needs more total CPU time than the encoder over a session
Its bursts are short, so it feels instant and barely delays the encoder
The encoder finishes sooner overall if it is interrupted more often
I/O-bound programs cannot be preempted, so the scheduler must run them first
why: An I/O-bound task runs briefly and then blocks again. Letting it run right away makes typing feel instant and costs the CPU-bound encoder only a tiny slice. Making it wait behind the encoder would add visible lag for almost no gain.
wrong: The editor uses very little CPU in total; it is mostly blocked waiting for input.
Extra interruptions add switches, which slightly slow the encoder.
Any thread can be preempted; the editor goes first because its bursts are short.
